source: Sio & Ormerod (2009) Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review (Psych Bull 135:94-120)
finding: Setting a problem aside gives a small but real gain over working on it without a break. The effect is heterogeneous across studies.
numbers: 117 independent effect sizes. Weighted random-effects mean d = 0.29, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.39. Unweighted mean 0.36 (SD 0.51). Cochran Q = 173.99, df 113, p<.001. Between-study variance 0.0834. Median 0.26.
limits: Mostly short lab breaks (minutes). Many small studies. Funnel plot judged symmetric, so no bias correction was applied.
agent_relevance: Break benefit is real but modest; an agent pause should be expected to give about 0.3 SD, not a breakthrough.

source: Sio & Ormerod (2009) Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review (Psych Bull 135:94-120): moderators
finding: Problem type matters. Divergent/creative tasks gain most from a break. Visual and linguistic insight problems gain less, and about equally (z = 1.25, ns).
numbers: Creative problems showed larger effects than visual and linguistic insight problems in the weighted regression (Table 9). Visual vs linguistic difference not significant.
limits: Task type is confounded with study era and lab. Few studies per cell for creative tasks.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a break helps convergent insight puzzles as much as idea-generation tasks. Use pauses mostly for generation.

source: Sio & Ormerod (2009) Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review (Psych Bull 135:94-120): preparation length
finding: The longer people struggled before the break, the bigger the incubation effect, for visual and creative problems but not for linguistic ones.
numbers: Correlation of prep time with weighted effect: visual r(35)=.40, p=.02; creative r(14)=.60, p=.03; linguistic r(65)=.04, p=.75.
limits: Correlational across studies, not manipulated within one study. Small k for creative.
agent_relevance: Supports 'impasse first, then pause': trigger a reset only after real effort has failed, not at step one.

source: Sio & Ormerod (2009) Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review (Psych Bull 135:94-120): filler task
finding: What fills the break matters only for linguistic insight problems: an undemanding filler beat plain rest. Demanding filler gave smaller gains than undemanding filler.
numbers: Linguistic subgroup (65 studies): low-demand task vs rest beta=.54, p<.05; interaction coefficient .45, p<.05. High load vs rest not different.
limits: Filler type coded from each paper's description. Rest sometimes allows deliberate thinking, which muddies the contrast.
agent_relevance: Break content may matter: a light, unrelated task between attempts is at least as good as idling.

source: Sio & Ormerod (2009) Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review (Psych Bull 135:94-120): theory test
finding: The pattern fits both spreading activation (linguistic) and restructuring (visual); the authors say no single mechanism explains all incubation.
numbers: Presence of solution-relevant cues during the break was not a significant moderator in the regressions.
limits: Mechanism inference from moderator regressions is weak.
agent_relevance: Design resets that work by several routes: drop the failed framing and re-seed with new associations.

source: Gilhooly (2016) Incubation and Intuition in Creative Problem Solving (Front Psychol 7:1076): intermittent work ruled out
finding: Three accounts of incubation: intermittent conscious work, beneficial forgetting, unconscious work. Checks on the filler task found no sign that people secretly kept working on the target.
numbers: Gilhooly et al. 2012/2015: no impairment of the interpolated tasks (mental rotation, anagrams). Across 8 correlations, 2 negative and 6 positive, mean r = 0.11; one significant r = .36, in the wrong direction for the intermittent-work account.
limits: Mostly divergent (alternative uses) tasks, one lab. Baird et al. 2012 thought sampling also found target-related thoughts did not predict gain.
agent_relevance: Secret rumination is not the cause; pause gains come from something else, so a plain context reset is a legitimate operator.

source: Gilhooly (2016) Incubation and Intuition in Creative Problem Solving (Front Psychol 7:1076): immediate incubation
finding: A break placed right after the instructions, before any work, also helps. That rules out beneficial forgetting of a fixation that never formed.
numbers: Strick et al. 2011 meta-analysis of immediate incubation: g = 0.224. Gilhooly 2012: immediate beat delayed incubation on alternative uses; both beat control.
limits: Dijksterhuis & Meurs 2006 task did not ask for unusual uses, so may measure recall of rare uses (Gilhooly says so).
agent_relevance: Even before trying, a pause or an unrelated first step can help generation tasks, but the effect is about 0.2 SD.

source: Gilhooly (2016) Incubation and Intuition in Creative Problem Solving (Front Psychol 7:1076): task similarity
finding: Dissimilar filler helps more than similar filler. The unconscious-work account predicts this; the forgetting account predicts the opposite.
numbers: Gilhooly et al. 2013 factorial: spatial filler helped a verbal divergent task more than verbal filler did, and verbal filler helped a spatial divergent task more than spatial filler. Significant interactions.
limits: Sample sizes not given in this review. Fatigue-recovery alternative (Ellwood 2009) not fully excluded.
agent_relevance: When interleaving, switch to a different representation or modality, not a near copy of the task.

source: Segal (2004) as reported by Gilhooly (2016): Fresh Look
finding: On a spatial insight problem after impasse, any break helped; length (4 vs 12 min) and demand (crossword vs browsing) made no difference. Supports a simple fresh look.
numbers: Break vs no break significant; no effect of break length or filler demand.
limits: Reported second-hand via the Gilhooly review. One problem.
agent_relevance: A cheap reset of attention may be enough; do not over-engineer the break.

source: Smith (1995) as reported by Gilhooly (2016): beneficial forgetting
finding: Misleading cues hurt, and people who forgot the misleading cue after a break solved more often. Forgetting grew with break length.
numbers: Qualitative: solving more likely when the misleading cue was forgotten; no numbers in the review.
limits: Second-hand; no numbers.
agent_relevance: Fixation cure: actively remove the failed attempt from context rather than only waiting.

source: Ritter & Dijksterhuis (2014) Creativity - the unconscious foundations of the incubation period (Front Hum Neurosci 8:215)
finding: Reviews incubation, mind wandering and sleep. Says many studies show only that a distraction helps and cannot separate unconscious work from mere distraction; the authors then argue for an unconscious contribution.
numbers: Field is mixed: strong effects in some studies (Kaplan 1989; Smith & Blankenship 1989), none in others (Olton & Johnson 1976). Dietrich & Kanso 2010 reviewed 72 neuroimaging studies and found no single region or process for creativity.
limits: Authors advocate unconscious thought theory; the review is partisan.
agent_relevance: Treat 'unconscious thought' as unproven; use incubation only as an empirical operator.

source: Ritter, van Baaren & Dijksterhuis (2012) Creativity: the role of unconscious processes in idea generation and idea selection (Thinking Skills & Creativity 7:21-27)
finding: A short distraction did not make ideas more creative or more numerous than deliberate thinking. It did help people pick their most creative idea.
numbers: Exp 1 (df 2,109, so N about 112): ideas count F(2,109)=5.43, p<.01, eta2=.09; immediate 3.89 < conscious 5.24 and unconscious 4.68; conscious vs unconscious ns. Creativity F<1. Selection chi2(2)=11.15, p<.01; unconscious beat conscious chi2(1)=5.67 and immediate chi2(1)=10.46. Exp 2 replicated selection (chi2(2)=8.00).
limits: Selection judged against rater consensus; one task (cash-desk waiting). Same lab family as the theory, not independent.
agent_relevance: A pause may help selecting among candidates more than generating them: put a pause before the pick step.

source: Nieuwenstein et al. (2015) On making the right choice: meta-analysis and large-scale replication of the unconscious thought advantage (Judgment and Decision Making 10:1-17)
finding: A large replication found no unconscious thought advantage in decisions, and the meta-analysis showed earlier positive results came from small underpowered studies.
numbers: Replication N = 399, designed under conditions judged optimal for the effect. No evidence of UTA; the gender-specific version also unsupported.
limits: Decision-making, not insight problems. Only the abstract page was read; k and pooled effect not seen.
agent_relevance: Caution: the 'let the unconscious work' story has a failed large replication in decisions. Do not build the schema on it.

source: Cai, Mednick, Harrison, Kanady & Mednick (2009) REM, not incubation, improves creativity by priming associative networks (PNAS 106:10130)
finding: On the Remote Associates Test, plain passage of time raised scores on repeated items about equally for REM nap, NREM nap and quiet rest. Only new, primed items showed a REM-specific gain.
numbers: 77 subjects (Exp 1 N=25: REM 10, NREM 6, rest 9; Exp 2 N=52: REM 18, NREM 6, rest 28). Group difference on repeated items P = 0.67. Improvement 95% CI: REM 6.5-38.3%, NREM 10.6-50.2%, rest 2.4-71.0%.
limits: Small cells (NREM n=6). Read as a fetched summary of the page, not full text.
agent_relevance: Time away alone is enough for repeated items; a sleep-like process is not needed for the basic effect.

source: Chein & Weisberg (2014) Working memory and insight in verbal problems: analysis of compound remote associates (Mem Cogn 42:67-83)
finding: Insight on CRA problems depends on working memory and attention control just as non-insight does. This speaks against a special unconscious process and for 'business as usual'.
numbers: N=53 (think-aloud 27, silent 26). Solved 24.75 of 60 (42%). 64% of solved problems rated insight. Verbal WM predicted overall solving (beta=.40, p=.03) and insight solutions (beta=.39, p=.03); spatial WM beta=-.01. Adding antisaccade lifted R2 from .19 to .39 overall and from .19 to .30 for insight solutions.
limits: One verbal problem type, university students, self-rated insight, correlational, moderate N.
agent_relevance: Insight-style solving uses the same limited control as plain reasoning, so scaffolds that protect working memory should help both.

source: Chein & Weisberg (2014) Working memory and insight in verbal problems: analysis of compound remote associates (Mem Cogn 42:67-83): speed and verbal overshadowing
finding: Problems rated insight were solved faster than analytic ones, which a late-and-sudden special process does not predict. Thinking aloud did not hurt.
numbers: Mean solution time 10.14 s (SD 6.06) insight vs 21.74 s (SD 6.16) analytic. Think-aloud vs silent: nearly identical solved counts and times (no verbal overshadowing).
limits: Fast solutions get an insight rating partly because they are fast, so the rating is confounded with speed.
agent_relevance: Written reasoning steps need not damage insight tasks; a visible-trace scaffold is acceptable.

source: Kizilirmak, Gallisch, Schott & Folta-Schoofs (2021) Insight is not always the same: true, false and induced insights in matchstick arithmetic (J Cog Psych)
finding: The Aha feeling does not guarantee a correct answer: true, false and induced insights differ in Aha rating, and the feeling did not fade over 40 trials.
numbers: 47 items. Mean 42.4% solved; 80.9% of correct solutions by the main route and 7.3% by an alternative. Aha rating lowest for false insights (mean 3.6). ERP differences 2000-1500 ms before the response.
limits: Matchstick arithmetic only. Participant N not extracted; ERP effects small.
agent_relevance: A felt 'aha' is an imperfect sign of correctness; the agent needs an external check, not a confidence feeling.

source: Henok, Vallee-Tourangeau & Vallee-Tourangeau (2020) Incubation and interactivity in insight problem solving (Psych Research 84:128-139): interactivity at time 1
finding: Acting on physical chain pieces lifted solving of the cheap necklace problem several-fold, and a 2-week break helped more for those who had interacted.
numbers: Exp 1: time 1 solved 43% (12) high interactivity vs 6% (2) low, chi2(1,N=63)=12.42, p<.001. Time 2 among earlier failures: 44% (7/16) vs 15% (5/33), chi2(1,N=49)=4.77, p=.029.
limits: One problem; 2-week gap is long.
agent_relevance: Letting the agent externalise and manipulate state (code, scratch objects) beats thinking in the head.

source: Henok, Vallee-Tourangeau & Vallee-Tourangeau (2020) Incubation and interactivity in insight problem solving (Psych Research 84:128-139): context at time 2
finding: After incubation, improvement depended on being able to act again. Switching to a hands-on version at time 2 gave big gains; switching to paper at time 2 did not.
numbers: Exp 2: time 1 solved 41% (14/34) high vs 15% (4/27) low, chi2(1,N=55)=5.03, p=.025. Time 2 among failures: 61% (14/23) after switching low to high; 5% (1/20) after switching high to low.
limits: Same problem, small cells. Favours an enactment account over pure incubation.
agent_relevance: The restart context matters more than the wait: re-enter with a richer interactive setup.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025/2026) Japanese children's riddles as a benchmark for machine insight and metacognition (NazoNazo, arXiv 2509.14704): accuracy
finding: LLMs do far worse than people on insight-style riddles. Reasoning models help but not enough; GPT-5 reached the human range.
numbers: 201 riddles; human reference on a 120-item subset, n=126, mean 52.9%. Non-reasoning models 7.6%, reasoning models 17.6%. Parameter count did not predict accuracy; release date did. Few-shot reasoning demonstrations improved all 4 tested models, significantly in 2.
limits: Japanese riddles; contamination possible; human sample is a subset.
agent_relevance: Insight problems are still hard for LLMs; measure scaffold gains on this kind of item.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025/2026) Japanese children's riddles as a benchmark for machine insight and metacognition (NazoNazo, arXiv 2509.14704): verification failure
finding: Models often write down the right answer during search, then do not commit and answer wrongly. Endorsement and stopping fail separately from generation.
numbers: Verification failures = 5.23% (Gemini 2.5 Flash) to 39.34% (Grok 4) of each model's wrong answers; 4 models with usable thought logs.
limits: Counted from thought logs; only some models expose them.
agent_relevance: Add a candidate register and a commit step based on evidence, since generation is not the only bottleneck.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025/2026) Japanese children's riddles as a benchmark for machine insight and metacognition (NazoNazo, arXiv 2509.14704): language of thought
finding: Reasoning in Japanese vs English changed accuracy for some models, not consistently.
numbers: Grok 4: Japanese 29.5% (33/112) vs English 48.8% (40/82), p=.0071. Claude Opus 4: 36.7% vs 28.7%, p=.356. Gemini 2.5 Flash: 0% vs 11.7%, p=.369.
limits: Language chosen by the model, not randomised; confounded with item difficulty.
agent_relevance: No strong case for forcing a thinking language.

source: d'Aliberti & Horta Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models (arXiv 2601.00514): prevalence and accuracy
finding: Spontaneous mid-reasoning shifts ('Wait, let me re-evaluate') are rare and go with lower accuracy, not higher. That argues against them being true restructuring.
numbers: 1M+ reasoning traces over training checkpoints, 3 domains (cryptic crosswords, math, Rush Hour). Qwen2.5-1.5B: shifts in about 7.6% of samples (6.31% pooled). Accuracy 2.57% for shifted vs 16.44% for non-shifted traces, N=723,200. Same pattern in DeepSeek-R1 and other external models.
limits: Mostly small models plus some larger ones; shift detection used an LLM judge.
agent_relevance: Do not count 'wait' tokens as insight; scaffold restructuring must be forced and checked.

source: d'Aliberti & Horta Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models (arXiv 2601.00514): entropy-gated forced reconsideration
finding: Forcing a second pass when the model is uncertain gives measured gains, while spontaneous shifts do not. This works like an externally triggered impasse and restart.
numbers: Pass 2 vs Pass 1: MATH-500 0.3221 to 0.4062 (+8.41 pp, N=320,000 pairs); crosswords 0.0970 to 0.1015 (+0.45 pp, N=83,200); Rush Hour near zero (0.000233 to 0.000363). Spontaneous shifts in math: raw -7.40 pp in high-entropy traces, -22.88 pp in low-entropy.
limits: Gains depend on domain and are tiny on crosswords and Rush Hour. Uses token entropy, not calibrated confidence.
agent_relevance: Supports an uncertainty-triggered 'second look' operator, but expect small gains on true insight puzzles.

source: Nair, Gizzi & Sinapov (2024) Creative problem solving in large language and vision models - what would it take? (arXiv 2405.01453)
finding: Preliminary test of creative object replacement ('what can replace a missing tool?'): models strong on ordinary cases, weak on creative replacements. Affordance information helped; task information alone often hurt.
numbers: Nominal cases above 90% for most CLIP models, ViLT 68%. Random pick about 30%. Creative replacement test lower, over 10 random object sets; task info mostly detrimental; task plus affordance not clearly better.
limits: Position paper with preliminary experiments; vision-language models (CLIP, ViLT), not chat LLMs; replacement numbers shown only in a figure.
agent_relevance: Describing object properties (affordances), not adding task text, is what lifts creative replacement; this fits restructuring.

source: Gilhooly (2016) overall verdict on meta-analyses
finding: From narrative reviews and meta-analyses, delayed incubation effects are established, especially for divergent tasks; mechanism remains open and the three accounts are not exclusive.
numbers: Sio & Ormerod mean d = 0.29; Strick et al. immediate incubation g = 0.224.
quote: The basic existence of Delayed Incubation effects is clearly established, especially for divergent problem solving.
limits: Author works on the unconscious-work account and tilts toward it.
agent_relevance: Design prior: try pauses for generation, expect d about 0.2 to 0.3.
